Yes, for any commit that gets replayed. A commit's hash covers its tree, parent hash, author, committer, timestamp, and message, so rebasing onto a new base changes the parent, which changes the hash, and that cascades to every descendant commit.

Exceptions: commits before the rebase point keep their hashes, and if the new base is the same as the old one (or git fast-forwards because nothing needs replaying), nothing changes. Even with an unchanged parent, `--force`/`--no-ff` or `-r`-style options, or edits like `reword`, `--reset-author`, or `--committer-date-is-author-date`, can alter hashes.

This is why rebasing already-pushed commits requires a force-push and disrupts collaborators.
